steps: From a reply to a booked call

check1.q: An owner’s week is clearly costing them, yet they keep putting off a decision. What is most likely at work?
o: They can’t afford it
Status quo bias: the familiar cost feels safer than an uncertain change
They don’t like the plans
They want a discount
check1.w: People prefer the situation they already have, even when it costs them. Make the cost of staying the same clear, and the risk of changing small.

check1.q: Which of these lowers trust the fastest?
o: Saying their words back to them
Admitting what Starter doesn’t include
Talking most of the call and moving quickly to the price
Recommending the smaller plan
check1.w: High self-orientation destroys trust. Listening, honesty about limits and recommending down all signal that you are there for them.

check1.q: How do we use scarcity honestly?
o: Tell every prospect a spot will be gone by Friday
Say once that Relève opens only 10 client spots a year, with the reason and the same count the website shows
Put the spot count in every follow-up email
Never mention it at all
check1.w: Scarcity is used only when it is true, once, with its reason. Never a false deadline, and never in emails, posts or follow-ups.

check1.q: Why do we present Specialist and Essential before recommending Starter?
o: To push owners toward the most expensive plan
Because Starter is a worse plan
Anchoring: after $4,500 and $2,500, $950 is heard as the easy first step it is
It is the order on the website
check1.w: The first number heard sets the scale. We anchor honestly, then recommend the plan that fits their audit.

check1.q: What is the test for whether a persuasion move is acceptable?
o: Whether it works
Whether the competition does it
Whether you’d be comfortable if the owner could see exactly what you were doing and why
Whether Sage would approve it later
check1.w: If you would be embarrassed to explain a move to the owner afterwards, don’t make it. That is the line between influence and manipulation.

check2.q: What should the first message to a new LinkedIn connection do?
o: Introduce Relève and the three plans
Ask an easy, interesting question about their week, without mentioning Relève
Share the pricing page
Ask for a call straight away
check2.w: The first message opens a conversation, peer to peer. Answering the question makes them name the cost before Relève has come up.

o: “Just circling back on my last message.”
“Checking in to see if you saw this.”
A short exercise they can use this week, with no ask attached
A third, fourth and fifth reminder
check2.w: Every follow-up adds value, and two is enough. Never “circling back,” “following up” or “checking in.”

check2.q: A prospect asks “how much?” in a LinkedIn message. What do you do?
o: Type out all three prices
Ignore the question
Point them to the plans on the website, and offer the audit to find the right fit
Offer a discount
check2.w: No prices in messages or posts. They live on the website, and the call is where we match a plan to their week.

o: A US agency owner with six staff who just posted that they’re hiring remote help
A manager inside a 2,000-person company
A UK coach with a solo practice
A clinic that needs a receptionist on site
check2.w: US owner, one to ten people, remote work, and a clear sign of need. The others fail on size, location or on-site work.

check2.q: What raises the chance that a booked call actually happens?
o: Sending the pricing page the day before
A short note the day before with one question about what they want from the call
Promising them a candidate on the call
A link into the app so they can look around
check2.w: A question they answer becomes a small commitment, and it tells you what to lead with. Never promise a candidate, and never link a prospect into the app.

check3.q: What is the upfront contract at the start of the call?
o: The Client Services Agreement
An agreement that at the end they will give a clear yes or no, and that no is fine
A promise of a candidate in 14 days
A list of prices
check3.w: Once someone agrees out loud to give a clear answer, “let me think about it” feels like going back on their word.

check3.q: During discovery, who should say what the problem is costing?
o: You, with an industry statistic
The owner, in their own words
Nobody: it’s rude to ask
The website
check3.w: Implication questions let the owner reach the conclusion. People believe their own conclusions far more than a seller’s.

check3.q: An owner has $30,000 a month in revenue, works 50 hours a week, and could hand off 12. Roughly what is that handoff worth each month?
o: About $1,200
About $3,600
About $7,176
About $30,000
check3.w: $30,000 ÷ (50 × 52 ÷ 12) is about $138 an hour. 12 hours × 52 ÷ 12 × $138 is about $7,176 a month.

check3.q: The owner says their last VA “never understood how I work.” Which front do you spend longest on?
o: Identity verified
The Relève Signature™, matched to how you work
Billing on the first Monday
The 14-day promise
check3.w: Match the front to their story. A working style problem is answered by the Signature on both sides.

check3.q: You’ve stacked the value and given the guarantee. What next?
o: Keep talking until they agree
Offer a discount
Stop talking and let them speak first
Move straight to the scarcity line
check3.w: Silence after a price is the hardest moment of the call. The first person to speak usually gives ground.

check4.q: An owner says, “It’s too expensive.” What is the best first response?
o: “Too expensive compared with what?”
“We can do a discount.”
“Everyone says that.”
“Our VAs are cheaper than local staff.”
check4.w: Find what they are comparing against. Then answer with their own numbers. Relève never makes cost claims.

check4.q: A prospect asks, “Can I see a few candidates first?” What do you say?
o: Send three profiles from the roster
Explain that we present one candidate, matched to how they work, so they never sort resumes, and that the next person comes forward if it isn’t right
Say yes after the call
Describe the best candidate on the roster
check4.w: One candidate is the service. Never present or describe a candidate before the search has opened.

check4.q: When is the best moment to plan the move from Starter to Essential?
o: After the three months are over
Never: let the client ask
In the live audit, with the later column, and again at the day 60 check-in
On the first invoice
check4.w: The later column plants it on the first call, and day 60 is when the owner feels the 15-hour cap. Matching someone with room to go full time keeps the same person.

check4.q: A maybe has gone three weeks with two follow-ups. What next?
o: Keep messaging every few days
A last, warm note that the audit and offer stand, then let The Relève Letter keep the relationship warm
Send the onboarding email anyway
Mark them as lost and delete them
check4.w: Generous, short and on a schedule. Pressure past that point costs goodwill, which is where later yeses and referrals come from.

check4.q: Your calls are happening, but almost none end in a yes. Where do you look first?
o: The connection note
Discovery: whether the cost was named, and whether a fit doubt was still open at the price
The website design
The day-before reminder
check4.w: Calls without a yes usually leak at discovery or the trial close. Listen back for where the second yes went missing.
